one_liner: Rust proc-macro lexer generator: compiles token/regex rules into one DFA with jump tables, aiming to beat hand-written lexers.
what_it_does: Logos is a derive macro (`#[derive(Logos)]`) that turns an enum annotated with `#[token(...)]`/`#[regex(...)]` variants into a full lexer, so you declare tokens instead of hand-writing a state machine. At compile time it generates the matching code via the logos-codegen crate; at runtime you call `Token::lexer(input)` and iterate to get `Result<Token, Error>` items with spans and slices. It targets building tokenizers for custom languages, config formats, and query languages in Rust.
how_it_is_fast: All token/regex rules are merged into a single deterministic finite automaton instead of being matched one-by-one, and branches in that DFA are compiled into lookup or jump tables. The codegen unrolls loops and batches byte reads to cut bounds checks, and disallows backtracking inside token definitions (avoiding ReDoS-style regex backtracking cost). All of this happens as proc-macro codegen at compile time, so the generated lexer has no runtime interpretation overhead.
when_to_use: Building a lexer for a DSL, config format, or query language in Rust and you want a declarative token spec instead of a hand-rolled state machine
Token set is a regular language expressible as literal tokens and regexes (identifiers, keywords, operators, punctuation, quoted strings)
Targeting no_std/embedded Rust (logos ships a no_std CI workflow) but still want compile-time generated matching
Want Criterion-verified throughput (README claims 1000+ MB/s on identifiers/strings) without hand-tuning SIMD yourself
Fine with proc-macro compile-time cost in exchange for a maintained, widely-used (3.6k-star) crate
when_not_to_use: Grammar needs backtracking, lookahead, or context-sensitive tokenization — logos explicitly forbids backtracking inside token definitions
Non-Rust project — this is a Rust crate/proc-macro, not usable from C/C++ or other toolchains

You need proof it beats a specific hand-written lexer: the project publishes no paired benchmark, and the only third-party paired test (alic.dev) shows logos losing ~10% to a naive hand lexer on x86_64 and 20-35% to an optimized SIMD hand lexer
You want to avoid unsafe code by default — logos uses unsafe internally unless you opt into the `forbid_unsafe` feature, which the README notes may cost performance
You want a single dependency-free source file to vendor — logos is a workspace of crates (logos, logos-derive, logos-codegen) driven by a proc-macro, not a drop-in header/source file

integration.dependencies: logos-derive (proc-macro, enabled via default `export_derive` feature); no required runtime deps beyond std (std feature can be disabled for no_std)
integration.platforms: any (no_std supported per CI workflow and crate keywords); no architecture-specific SIMD requirement documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces hand-written lexer logic but requires rewriting token definitions as a derive-macro enum, not a source-level drop-in

gotchas: Default build relies on unsafe code internally; the `forbid_unsafe` Cargo feature swaps in safe alternatives but the README/Cargo.toml note this may reduce performance
Backtracking inside token definitions is disallowed by design, so overlapping/ambiguous patterns need manual priority handling (see the book's token-disambiguation page)
A `state_machine_codegen` feature switches between two different codegen backends (tailcall vs. state-machine); behavior and performance can differ between them

The repo's own bench suite (tests/benches/bench.rs, run via CodSpeed CI) only benchmarks logos itself — no hand-written baseline is run in the same harness, so the README's 'ridiculously fast' framing is not a paired comparison
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick logos when you want a general-purpose, actively maintained Rust lexer generator with an ergonomic derive-macro API and broad adoption (3.6k stars) rather than a domain-specific tool like CrossDB (SQL only) or Accelerated-Zig-Parser (Zig compiler internals); pick a hand-written or SIMD-tuned lexer instead (e.g. dist1ll's lexer-exp, which reports beating logos by ~35% on Apple M1) when raw throughput against a tuned baseline matters more than developer ergonomics.
verified_claims_summary: Logos's README reports only its own Criterion throughput (identifiers 1204 MB/s, strings 1575 MB/s, keywords/operators/punctuators 1037 MB/s) with no baseline lexer measured in the same run and no hardware or rustc version given. The one paired comparison found, a third-party blog (alic.dev) on an Apple M1 tokenizing a 100KB pseudocode file, showed logos beating a naive hand-written lexer ~1.8x (174,476 vs 312,837 ns/iter) but running about 10% slower than that same hand lexer on an unspecified x86_64 CPU (221,110 vs 201,148 ns/iter); the author's later SIMD-optimized (NEON) hand-written lexer beat logos by 20-35%.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-11, v0.16.1 on crates.io, 3,566 stars) and dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed, so it's low-risk to depend on directly; it is an ordinary Cargo dependency rather than a header-only file, so 'copyable' here means small enough to vendor, not a single-file drop-in.
